sentences.text: The genus Zhuchengtitan contains only one species, Z. zangjiazhuangensis, which was named in 2017 based on a single humerus — the upper arm bone.
This animal is known from a single humerus discovered in the Wangshi Group near Zhucheng, Shandong, China.
The top end of the humerus is 0.55 times the length of the entire bone, a proportion extreme compared to other titanosaurs.
This extreme width arises because the inner edge angles more sharply inwards at the top than at the bottom.
The prominent deltopectoral crest, a ridge for muscle attachment, bears a hook-like process extending about halfway down its length.
This crest extends down to the midshaft and sideways to occupy the outer width of the bone.
The humerus fossil is mostly complete but has suffered significant damage to the outer edges of the top and bottom ends and the deltopectoral crest.
Zhuchengtitan is distinguished from other Asian titanosaurids like Qingxiusaurus and Huabeisaurus by a wider humeral head and a more developed deltopectoral crest.
Researchers uncovered the humerus and other sauropod bones at the Zangjiazhuang Quarry in 2008.
The fossil was discovered in 2008 by researchers at the Zhucheng Dinosaur Research and Culture Center at the Zangjiazhuang quarry.
The humerus was catalogued with the number ZJZ-57.
The species was formally described in 2017 by Mo Jinyou, Wang Kebai, Chen Shuqing, Wang Peiye, and Xu Xing.
The genus name Zhuchengtitan combines the location Zhucheng with the Greek suffix titan.
Thousands of Shantungosaurus fossils found at the site likely represent victims of a sudden mass mortality event.
Mo and colleagues assigned Zhuchengtitan to the family Saltasauridae based on specific humeral traits.
Researchers hypothesized that Zhuchengtitan may be closely related to Opisthocoelicaudia, but noted this needs confirmation from additional fossils.
Dating of a basalt layer places the Hongtuya Member at 73.5 million years old, corresponding to the Campanian age of the Cretaceous.
Zhuchengtitan lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, approximately 72 million years ago, during the Maastrichtian.
Zhuchengtitan inhabited environments characterized by alluvial fans, braided rivers, and floodplains.
